hints: Integrate acceleration $a(t) = k(16 - t^2)$ to find velocity: $v(t) = k\left(16t - \frac{1}{3}t^3\right) + C$. Use $v(0) = 0$ to get $C = 0$.
Use $v(4) = 8$ to determine $k$: $8 = k\left(64 - \frac{64}{3}\right) = k\left(\frac{128}{3}\right) \implies k = \frac{3}{16}$.
Integrate $v(t) = 3t - \frac{1}{16}t^3$ to find displacement $s(t)$, with $s(0) = 0$, and factor out $\frac{1}{64}t^2$ to show $s = \frac{1}{64}t^2(96 - t^2)$.
walkthrough:
State the relationship between velocity and acceleration: velocity is the integral of acceleration with respect to time:
$$v(t) = \int a(t)\,dt = \int k(16 - t^2)\,dt = k\left(16t - \frac{t^3}{3}\right) + C_1$$

Apply the initial condition: particle $P$ starts from rest at $O$, so $v(0) = 0$ when $t = 0$:
$$0 = k(0 - 0) + C_1 \implies C_1 = 0$$
Thus:
$$v(t) = k\left(16t - \frac{1}{3}t^3\right)$$

Use the condition that $v = 8\text{ m s}^{-1}$ when $t = 4\text{ s}$:
$$8 = k\left(16(4) - \frac{4^3}{3}\right) = k\left(64 - \frac{64}{3}\right)$$
$$8 = k\left(\frac{192 - 64}{3}\right) = k\left(\frac{128}{3}\right)$$
Multiply both sides by $3$ and divide by $128$:
$$k = \frac{24}{128} = \frac{3}{16}$$

Write out the simplified velocity function:
$$v(t) = \frac{3}{16}\left(16t - \frac{1}{3}t^3\right) = 3t - \frac{1}{16}t^3$$

Integrate velocity with respect to $t$ to obtain displacement $s(t)$:
$$s(t) = \int v(t)\,dt = \int \left(3t - \frac{1}{16}t^3\right)\,dt = \frac{3t^2}{2} - \frac{t^4}{16 \times 4} + C_2 = \frac{3}{2}t^2 - \frac{1}{64}t^4 + C_2$$

Apply the condition that $P$ starts at $O$, so $s(0) = 0$:
$$0 = 0 - 0 + C_2 \implies C_2 = 0$$
Factor out $\frac{1}{64}t^2$:
$$s(t) = \frac{1}{64}t^2\left(\frac{3 \times 64}{2} - t^2\right) = \frac{1}{64}t^2(96 - t^2)$$
Thus $s = \frac{1}{64}t^2(96 - t^2)$ as required.

hints: The particle returns to $O$ when displacement $s = 0$ for $t > 0$.
Substitute $t = \sqrt{96}$ into the velocity function $v(t) = 3t - \frac{1}{16}t^3$, and state the speed as a positive magnitude.
walkthrough:
Find the time when particle $P$ returns to the origin $O$ by setting displacement $s(t) = 0$:
$$\frac{1}{64}t^2(96 - t^2) = 0$$
For $t > 0$, divide by $\frac{1}{64}t^2$:
$$96 - t^2 = 0 \implies t^2 = 96 \implies t = \sqrt{96} = 4\sqrt{6} \approx 9.79796\text{ s}$$

Substitute $t = \sqrt{96}$ into the velocity formula $v(t) = 3t - \frac{1}{16}t^3$:
$$v = 3\sqrt{96} - \frac{1}{16}(\sqrt{96})^3$$
Notice that $(\sqrt{96})^3 = 96\sqrt{96}$:
$$v = 3\sqrt{96} - \frac{96}{16}\sqrt{96} = 3\sqrt{96} - 6\sqrt{96} = -3\sqrt{96}$$

Simplify the exact radical expression:
$$-3\sqrt{96} = -3\sqrt{16 \times 6} = -3(4\sqrt{6}) = -12\sqrt{6}\text{ m s}^{-1}$$

State the speed as the absolute magnitude of velocity:
$$\text{Speed} = |v| = 12\sqrt{6} \approx 29.3939\text{ m s}^{-1}$$
Rounding to three significant figures gives:
$$\text{Speed} = 29.4\text{ m s}^{-1}$$
Thus the speed of $P$ at the instant that it returns to $O$ is $29.4\text{ m s}^{-1}$.

hints: Displacement is at a stationary point (maximum) when velocity $v(t) = 0$.
Substitute $t^2 = 48$ into $s = \frac{1}{64}t^2(96 - t^2)$ to evaluate the maximum displacement.
walkthrough: State the condition for maximum displacement: maximum displacement occurs at an instantaneous turning point where velocity is zero ($v = 0$) and acceleration is negative ($\frac{dv}{dt} < 0$).

Set $v(t) = 0$:
$$3t - \frac{1}{16}t^3 = 0$$
Factor out $t$:
$$t\left(3 - \frac{1}{16}t^2\right) = 0$$
For $t > 0$:
$$3 - \frac{1}{16}t^2 = 0$$
$$\frac{1}{16}t^2 = 3$$
Multiply by $16$:
$$t^2 = 48 \implies t = \sqrt{48} = 4\sqrt{3}\text{ s}$$

Substitute $t^2 = 48$ into the displacement formula $s = \frac{1}{64}t^2(96 - t^2)$:
$$s_{\text{max}} = \frac{1}{64}(48)(96 - 48)$$
Compute the terms:
$$96 - 48 = 48$$
$$s_{\text{max}} = \frac{1}{64}(48)(48) = \frac{2304}{64} = 36\text{ m}$$
Thus the maximum displacement of the particle from $O$ is $36\text{ m}$.
